To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the chemical form (phospholipid or triglyceride) of DHA consumed during pregnancy did not affect the DHA content in the maternal and fetal tissues including fetal brain, and that the phospholipid form of DHA enhanced dietary fat absorption.

the chemical structure of the DHA source did not differentially affect the DHA accreted into the fetal brain, and that DHA consumption as PL did not improve its incorporation into rat fetal brain, compared to the triglyceride (TG) form.
the chemical form (PL or TG form) of DHA consumed during pregnancy does not differentially alter the incorporation of DHA into the fetal brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical form of dietary DHA during pregnancy.
the effect that different DHA-containing lipid sources have on the DHA content of maternal and fetal tissues during gestation in a rodent model.
the chemical form of dietary DHA supplementation during gestation, which may influence the placental uptake and fetal brain incorporation of this essential fatty acid.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the chemical form (PL or TG), the amount of DHA, the amount of PLs in the diet, and the amount of dietary fat are important factors that influence DHA accretions in the fetus, and that all of these factors must be carefully considered when designing a DHA supplementation program for pregnant women.
the chemical form in which DHA is provided to the mother during pregnancy (PL or TG), does not affect the fetal DHA content in the brain.
the PL and TG forms of DHA supplementation in pregnant rats are equally effective in ensuring adequate fetal DHA supply.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the chemical form in which DHA is consumed by the rat mother during gestation does not differentially influence the DHA accreted by the fetus, and both lipid structures can be equally used as a source of maternal DHA supplementation.
the chemical form (TG or PL) of DHA does not influence the placental transfer of DHA, and therefore, the DHA content in the brain of fetuses from rats that were supplemented with DHA as TG or PL.
the chemical form in which the DHA is supplied during pregnancy does not affect its availability for fetal DHA incorporation into brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PLs are more efficiently absorbed than TGs, but the DHA content in fetal brain is not increased when the DHA-PL diet contains a high PL content.
DHA-PLs and DHA-TGs are equally effective in improving maternal and fetal DHA status.
DHA consumption during gestation as phospholipid did not improve the DHA content of maternal and fetal tissues compared to triglycerides.
